precepts.text: Seven: the golden calf. As for this Moses, we wot not what is become of him: listen to the disrespect toward the man who led them out. Aaron made the calf out of fear, knowing better as high priest, and the people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play in honour of a god that cannot talk. No difference from our people today who prefer white Jesus or run to a stone in the east that cannot answer prayers.
precepts.point: Because all those men which have seen my glory and my miracles have tempted me now these ten times, and have not hearkened to my voice. Write the ten down; the Most High deals in numbers, and nothing in the Bible is insignificant.

note.label: 70 Times 7: The Perfection of Mercy Through Christ

precepts.why:
Number seven is the golden calf. “And when the people saw that Moses delayed to come down out of the mount, the people gathered themselves together unto Aaron, and said unto him, Up, make us gods, which shall go before us; for as for this Moses, the man that brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we wot not what is become of him.”

That is the no gratitude. The Most High just showed all those wonderful plagues and destroyed your enemy, and now you want a different god, a god of silver, gold and wood, a god that cannot talk. And look how disrespectful: as for this Moses. No different from our people who despise this truth and want to go back to Christianity, who prefer white Jesus, or who run to the east, to Mecca, and pray to a damn cobblestone that cannot talk back or answer prayers. That is why the Most High says we are dumber than an ox.

Aaron, the high priest, got real simple here, but it was out of fear, and he knew better. Then, “he received them at their hand, and fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf”; he had the skills of a blacksmith and turned the gold they spoiled from Egypt into idolatry. It was the people who said “These be thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.” Then “the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play”: in honour of that pagan god they had orgies.

“They have turned aside quickly out of the way which I commanded them”. “I have seen this people, and, behold, it is a stiffnecked people: Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them, and that I may consume them”. Yes, we are a stiffnecked people, and only Moses standing in the gap turned it away, as he did again in Numbers 14.

precepts.text: These things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted. Why were they overthrown in the wilderness? Because they lusted after evil things. Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed, and fell in one day three and twenty thousand. The rose up to play was fornication, and it destroyed us. The nations understood this when they took their crafty counsel.
precepts.point: The people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play. That rose up to play was not hopscotch.

note.label: Pay The Price: Pleasure Now Regret Later

precepts.why:
At the golden calf “the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play.” What was that rose up to play? You think it was hopscotch? Paul explains it.

“Neither be ye idolaters, as were some of them; as it is written, The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” He is quoting the very verse, and before it he says: “Now these things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted.” When they lusted after evil things, that is the rose up to play.

The verse before that: “But with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness.” Why were they overthrown in the wilderness? Because they lusted after evil things.

Then verse 8: “Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed, and fell in one day three and twenty thousand.” So we understand the rose up to play was fornication. They lusted after evil things, and it destroyed us.

The nations understood this. When we are in sin, they know what will happen, they can destroy us. So when they took their crafty counsel they said, how do we keep these people in error? They like to rap, so give them murder music and lascivious music. That is why they give our sisters these songs, so vulgar. Their whole plan is to keep us in sin. Pleasure now, regret later: you are going to pay.

precepts.text: All our fathers were under the cloud and were baptized unto Moses, and that Rock was Christ; the Corinthians were Israelites. Neither be ye idolaters, as it is written, the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.
precepts.point: Aaron built an altar before it and made proclamation, To morrow is a feast to the LORD; and the people rose up early, offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play. Israel kept provoking God, and the Lord still brought the nation into the promised land as he promised Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

note.label: Exodus 32: The Golden Calf at Horeb

precepts.why:
Paul writes to the Corinthians: “all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea; And were all baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea”, and “they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ.” Our fathers: the Corinthians were Israelites.

“But with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness. Now these things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things, as they also lusted. Neither be ye idolaters, as were some of them; as it is written, The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” That is the golden calf: Aaron's altar, the feast to the Lord, the burnt offerings and peace offerings, and the people rising up to play.

Israel kept provoking God, and the Lord still brought the nation into the promised land as he promised Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. But the calf is written as our example, so that we do not become idolaters as some of them were.

precepts.text: Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God; the evil still in a man from the world will corrupt him as it did our forefathers.
precepts.point: Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them, and that I may consume them: and I will make of thee a great nation. Moses was of the tribe of Levi, of the seed of Jacob, so the Lord could have started over with him.

note.label: Exodus 32: The Golden Calf at Horeb

precepts.why:
“Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools: for they consider not that they do evil.”

Not forty days gone, and Israel had already turned aside quickly out of the way, made a molten calf and worshipped it. The spirit that was in Israel in Egypt was still in Israel when they left. They considered not that they did evil; they thought they were giving a sacrifice.

It is the same coming into this truth. The evil carried in from the world will corrupt you and turn you from the Lord if it is not put off, as it did our forefathers. Without the laws of God we are a carnal, rebellious, stiffnecked people, so these last days call for humbleness and repentance, being more ready to hear, not bringing the world's rhetoric into the congregation.

precepts.text: Declaring the end from the beginning; my counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure.
precepts.point: From the questions: the Lord dealt with Moses on a level where Moses could speak to him so, but the outcome stood on what was declared from the beginning; had it been his pleasure to destroy, nothing Moses said could have stayed it.

note.label: Exodus 32: The Golden Calf at Horeb

precepts.why:
“Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times the things that are not yet done, saying, My counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure”.

“And the Lord repented of the evil which he thought to do unto his people.” The Most High does not repent as a man; he has no one to answer to. He simply turned from the anger of that moment. He was never going to break his covenant, for consuming the people would have destroyed all the seed of Jacob except Moses, and he had sworn by his own self to Abraham, Isaac and Israel to multiply their seed as the stars of heaven. Moses was there to remind him of his own word.

The Lord dealt with Moses on a level where Moses could speak to him so, but the outcome stood on what was declared from the beginning. Had it been his pleasure to destroy, nothing Moses said could have stayed it: my counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure.

precepts.text: They soon forgat his works and waited not for his counsel, but lusted exceedingly in the wilderness, and tempted God in the desert.
precepts.point: The psalm gives the depth of it: they soon forgat his works and waited not for his counsel, they made a calf in Horeb and changed their glory into the similitude of an ox that eateth grass, and they forgat God their saviour, which had done great things in Egypt, wondrous works in the land of Ham, and terrible things by the Red sea.

note.label: Exodus 32: The Golden Calf at Horeb

precepts.why:
Aaron told Moses, “thou knowest the people, that they are set on mischief.” The psalm gives the depth of it: “They soon forgat his works; they waited not for his counsel: But lusted exceedingly in the wilderness, and tempted God in the desert.”

They would not wait for Moses to come down from the mount, and they would not wait for the Lord's counsel. “And he gave them their request; but sent leanness into their soul. They envied Moses also in the camp, and Aaron the saint of the Lord.” That is the camp Moses came back to, deep in wickedness; and Aaron, left in charge, could not blame the congregation for it, for the charge has to be carried.

precepts.text: They made a calf in Horeb and forgat God their saviour; he said he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen stood before him in the breach, to turn away his wrath.
precepts.point: The psalm gives the depth of it: they soon forgat his works and waited not for his counsel, they made a calf in Horeb and changed their glory into the similitude of an ox that eateth grass, and they forgat God their saviour, which had done great things in Egypt, wondrous works in the land of Ham, and terrible things by the Red sea.

note.label: Exodus 32: The Golden Calf at Horeb

precepts.why:
“They made a calf in Horeb, and worshipped the molten image. Thus they changed their glory into the similitude of an ox that eateth grass.” Aaron said, “I cast it into the fire, and there came out this calf”; the psalm says what that calf was: Israel trading their glory for the likeness of an ox that eats grass.

“They forgat God their saviour, which had done great things in Egypt; Wondrous works in the land of Ham, and terrible things by the Red sea.” All of that so soon forgotten. “Therefore he said that he would destroy them, had not Moses his chosen stood before him in the breach, to turn away his wrath, lest he should destroy them.”

A leader cannot blame the congregation, the same excuse Saul gave. Moses, the leader who carried the charge, stood in the breach for the very people who envied him.

precepts.text: I am the LORD thy God; thou shalt have no other gods before me, nor make any graven image, nor bow down to them, for the iniquity of the fathers is visited upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate him; the calf broke these first commandments.
precepts.point: The Lord answered, Whosoever hath sinned against me, him will I blot out of my book; therefore now go, lead the people, and mine Angel shall go before thee; nevertheless in the day when I visit I will visit their sin upon them. And the LORD plagued the people, because they made the calf, which Aaron made.

note.label: Exodus 32: The Golden Calf at Horeb

precepts.why:
“Ye have sinned a great sin.” The commandments had just been given at Sinai: “I am the Lord thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage. Thou shalt have no other gods before me. Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath”, and “Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them”.

The calf broke the first two commandments: they made themselves gods of gold, a graven image, and bowed down and served it. And the Lord had already said how He would deal with it: “I the Lord thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me”. So He told Moses, “in the day when I visit I will visit their sin upon them.”

precepts.text: The Most High himself said, I have seen this people, and, behold, it is a stiffnecked people.
precepts.point: Israel became a burden to Moses to the point he asked the Most High to kill him rather than let him see his own wretchedness. While I am yet alive with you this day, ye have been rebellious against the Lord; and how much more after my death?

note.label: Deuteronomy 31: Moses' Final Charge and the Rebellion Foretold

precepts.why:
“For I know thy rebellion, and thy stiff neck”. A stiff neck means you are told what to do and you refuse to do it. If anybody knew Israel's rebellion, Moses knew, and the Most High himself said the same at the golden calf: “I have seen this people, and, behold, it is a stiffnecked people”.

Israel kept that spirit even after judgments, miracles and harsh consequences. Moses saw it for forty years, so he could say “while I am yet alive with you this day, ye have been rebellious against the Lord; and how much more after my death?”

precepts.text: Who is on the Lord's side? All the sons of Levi gathered unto Moses and did according to his word, and there fell that day about three thousand men.
precepts.point: At the golden calf, when Moses stood in the gate of the camp and said, Who is on the Lord's side? let him come unto me, only the sons of Levi gathered themselves unto him. They took every man his sword and did according to the word of Moses without hesitating, and there fell of the people that day about three thousand men. That is why the blessing says they saw not father or mother nor acknowledged their brethren: that is the devotion they had for the covenant.

note.label: Deuteronomy 33: The Blessing of Moses, Identifying the Tribes in the Last Days

precepts.why:
“Who said unto his father and to his mother, I have not seen him; neither did he acknowledge his brethren, nor knew his own children: for they have observed thy word, and kept thy covenant.” This is the zeal Levi had for the Most High, and it was shown at the golden calf: “Then Moses stood in the gate of the camp, and said, Who is on the Lord’s side? let him come unto me. And all the sons of Levi gathered themselves together unto him.” Only the sons of Levi gathered.

“Put every man his sword by his side, and go in and out from gate to gate throughout the camp, and slay every man his brother, and every man his companion, and every man his neighbour. And the children of Levi did according to the word of Moses: and there fell of the people that day about three thousand men.” They took every man his sword and did it without hesitating: brother, companion and neighbour. That is why the blessing says they saw not father or mother nor acknowledged their brethren; that is the devotion they had for the covenant.

precepts.text: Moses broke the first tables when he came down from the mount and saw the people dancing before the golden calf they had made from their gold earrings.
precepts.point: So what is the ark of the covenant, and what does it contain? The Lord told Moses to hew two tables of stone like the first ones he broke, and the Lord rewrote the ten commandments on them with his own finger, and Moses put the tables in the ark. The ark of the covenant contained the commandments that God wrote.

note.label: 1 Samuel 4: The Ark of God Is Taken

precepts.why:
The first tables were broken. Moses came down, and “as soon as he came nigh unto the camp, that he saw the calf, and the dancing: and Moses’ anger waxed hot, and he cast the tables out of his hands, and brake them beneath the mount.” The people were dancing before the golden calf they had made from their gold earrings.

That is why the Lord told Moses to hew two tables of stone like the first ones he broke, and the Lord rewrote the ten commandments on them with his own finger.

note.label: When Good Intentions Lead To Bad Judgement In Israel

precepts.why: “But with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness.” “Now these things were our examples, to the intent we should not lust after evil things”. That whole thing happened as an example so we wouldn't lust after evil things as our forefathers did. “Neither be ye idolaters, as were some of them”. They had those calves and were idolatrous. “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” Fornication, reveling, idolatry—all type of evil was going on. “Neither let us commit fornication, as some of them committed, and fell in one day three and twenty thousand.” Twenty-three thousand people fell in the wilderness, put to death for that foolishness.

note.label: When Good Intentions Lead To Bad Judgement In Israel

precepts.why: “I am the Lord your God.” “After the doings of the land of Egypt, wherein ye dwelt, shall ye not do”. “and after the doings of the land of Canaan, whither I bring you, shall ye not do: neither shall ye walk in their ordinances.” Don't follow what they do. Our forefathers came out of Egypt following the garbage they followed there. That's why they made the golden calves; that's what they knew. As soon as Moses disappeared, we went right back to the evil our slave masters had us doing.

note.label: Bishop Nathanyel | Revelation 3 A Message to The 7 Churches

precepts.why: Naked. What does it mean by naked? “And when Moses saw that the people were naked; (for Aaron had made them naked unto their shame among their enemies:)” So when the Bible calls you naked, it says you are naked to your shame. That is what it is making reference to: you are naked to shame.

note.label: When Good Intentions Lead To Bad Judgement In Israel

points: “Wherefore should the Egyptians speak, and say, For mischief did he bring them out”. Moses is telling the Lord not to destroy us; the Egyptians will laugh and say he brought us out for nothing. Moses is talking to him face to face, trying to calm him down. Lord, you're mad as hell right now, but don't forget your promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
“Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, thy servants”. “I will multiply your seed as the stars of heaven”. Remember the promise that their seed would inherit the land forever.

note.label: When Good Intentions Lead To Bad Judgement In Israel

points: “And the Lord repented of the evil which he thought to do unto his people.” The Lord calmed down. All right, Moses, you're right; I promised I wouldn't destroy them. He was up there giving Moses righteous laws for us to live by, to make us special people and his children, and we were down there worshipping a calf, having sex, fornication, adultery, and all type of evil. He was mad. He still killed 23,000, but he didn't kill the whole nation of Israel.

note.label: When Good Intentions Lead To Bad Judgement In Israel

points: “Oh, this people have sinned a great sin, and have made them gods of gold.” Moses was going in on them, not playing with them, slaying them. “blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written.” You know how heavy that is? Lord, blot me out of the book; just keep the promise you made to them. That's the mindset we're supposed to have for our people.

note.label: When Good Intentions Lead To Bad Judgement In Israel

points: “Whosoever hath sinned against me, him will I blot out of my book.” I ain't going to blot you out, Moses. Whoever broke my laws and disobeyed me, that's the one I'm putting to death and taking out of the book of life.

note.label: When Good Intentions Lead To Bad Judgement In Israel

points: “nevertheless in the day when I visit I will visit their sin upon them.” I ain't going to forget what they did, Moses. I'm going to hold it against them. “And the Lord plagued the people, because they made the calf, which Aaron made.” That's how he plagued them: he killed 23,000. He wasn't playing with us. Aaron did it under the guise of good intentions, but it was terrible judgment to make golden calves when the Lord had just brought us out of Egypt and set him up as priest.
